newsitem.title: GERMANY: Rato says hard to define stability pact exceptions.
newsitem.headline: Rato says hard to define stability pact exceptions.

text.p: Spain's Economy Minister Rodrigo Rato said on Friday that setting a numerical definition for granting countries exemptions from sanctions under a proposed European stability pact would be very difficult.
Europe is trying to agree on terms for a "stability pact" which will ensure that nations which join their currencies in the Euro maintain fiscal discipline long-term.

Germany has been very vocal in insisting that there must be a precise numerical definition of exactly what constitutes a "temporary and exceptional" economic circumstance which would allow a country to run an over-high budget deficit.
The German delegation wants a strict definition stating that an economy would have to contract by at least two percent in the course of a year for an exceptional circumstance to be declared.
Rato said in an interview with Reuters Financial Television at a banking congress in Frankfurt that Spain supported the idea of a clear definition, but was reluctant to have specific figures set.

"It should be a clear cut definition, but it is probably very difficult to make it in numbers, because the differences between the business cycles in the future and the differences between countries will probably recommend a definition which states that extraordinary circumstances have to be really extraordinary," he said.
"In numerical terms there should just be a reference but not a closed definition," he added.
Germany, supported by some other countries, has opposed such a vague ruling on the grounds that it would be too easily open to abuse.

Rato added however that there should be clear rules in some areas. "Temporary should be defined. The discussion now in the Ecofin is between one and two years and we think that is a reasonable time," he said.

On the prospects of Spain joining European monetary union in 1999 with the first round, Rato said, "I am sure that the Spanish situation and determination to fulfill the Maastricht criteria are very clear. They are reconised by the market and backed by major political forces and society.
"Spain is certainly increasing its chances to fulfill all the criteria", he added.
